rules.title: One equals sign or two?
rules.say: “= checks if two things are equal.”
rules.truth: A single = stores a value. Two equals signs == ask a question.
rules.tip: Read = as “becomes” and == as “is equal to?”.

rules.title: Don't forget the colon
rules.say: “The line is complete without the colon.”
rules.truth: if, for, while, def and class lines end with a colon. It tells Python a block follows.
rules.tip: Block starters end in :

rules.title: print needs brackets
rules.say: “print is a keyword you can write without brackets.”
rules.truth: In Python 3, print is a function, so you call it with ( ).
rules.tip: Functions are always called with ( ).

rules.title: Indentation is the structure
rules.say: “Spaces are just for looks.”
rules.truth: In Python the spaces at the start of a line decide which block the line belongs to.
rules.tip: Lines in the same block start in the same column.

rules.title: input() always gives text
rules.say: “If I type 5, I get the number 5.”
rules.truth: input() returns a string. "5" + 1 is an error, and "10" < 9 is not allowed. Convert with int() or float() first.
rules.tip: Typed in = text. Wrap with int() when you need a number.

rules.title: Text and numbers don't mix with +
rules.say: “+ glues anything together.”
rules.truth: + adds numbers or joins two strings, not one of each. Turn the number into text with str(), or use an f-string.
rules.tip: f"...{value}..." is the easy way to mix text and numbers.

match.msg: can only concatenate str \(not \"int\"\) to str|must be str, not int

rules.title: Names must match exactly
rules.say: “Python will work out what I meant.”
rules.truth: A name only exists after you create it, and it must be spelled the same every time, including capital letters.
rules.tip: Copy-paste names instead of retyping them.

rules.title: Strings can't be edited in place
rules.say: “word[0] = 'B' changes the first letter.”
rules.truth: Strings are fixed once made. Build a new string instead.
rules.tip: To change text, make new text.

match.msg: 'str' object does not support item assignment

rules.title: Missing dictionary keys crash
rules.say: “A missing key just gives nothing.”
rules.truth: Reading a key that is not there raises KeyError. Use .get(key, default) or check with in first.
rules.tip: d[key] demands the key. d.get(key, default) is polite.

rules.title: range stops one early (and lists start at 0)
rules.say: “Indexes run from 1 to len.”
rules.truth: A list of n items has indexes 0 to n-1. range(n) gives 0 to n-1, so range(len(x) + 1) walks off the end.
rules.tip: Last index = len - 1. range(a, b) never includes b.

rules.title: sort() changes the list, it does not return it
rules.say: “x = nums.sort() gives me the sorted list.”
rules.truth: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None. Use sorted(nums) when you want a new sorted list.
rules.tip: sort() = change it. sorted() = give me a new one.

rules.title: append() returns None
rules.say: “nums = nums.append(4) gives me the longer list.”
rules.truth: append changes the list in place and returns None, so the variable becomes None. Just call nums.append(4).
rules.tip: Methods that change a list usually return None.

rules.title: print shows it, return gives it back
rules.say: “print() hands the answer back to the caller.”
rules.truth: print() only shows text on the screen. A function must return its answer, otherwise the caller gets None.
rules.tip: If another line of code needs the value, return it.

rules.title: / always gives a decimal
rules.truth: / always returns a float, so 10 / 2 is 5.0. Use // for whole-number division.
rules.tip: // divides and drops the remainder.

rules.title: Don't change a list while looping over it
rules.say: “Removing items inside the loop is fine.”
rules.truth: The loop keeps counting positions while the list shrinks, so it skips items. Loop over a copy, or build a new list.
rules.right: nums = [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]
rules.tip: Build a new list instead of editing the one you are walking through.

rules.title: is is not ==
rules.say: “is means equal.”
rules.truth: is asks whether two names point at the very same object, not whether the values match. Use == to compare values.
rules.tip: Compare values with ==. Use is only for None.

rules.title: A default list is shared by every call
rules.say: “A fresh [] is made for every call.”
rules.truth: A default value is built once, when the function is defined. Every call that uses it shares the same list.
rules.tip: Use None as the default, then make the list inside.

rules.title: The loop never ends
rules.say: “The loop will stop by itself.”
rules.truth: A while loop runs as long as its condition stays true. Something inside the loop must change the thing the condition checks.
rules.tip: Ask: what changes each time round? If nothing, it never stops.

rules.title: int() needs digits
rules.say: “int() reads any text as a number.”
rules.truth: int("abc") and int("3.5") raise ValueError. Check the text first, or catch the error with try / except.
rules.tip: Wrap risky conversions in try / except ValueError.

rules.title: NULL is not a value you can compare with =
rules.say: “WHERE phone = NULL finds the missing ones.”
rules.truth: Nothing equals NULL, not even NULL. Ask with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.
rules.wrong: SELECT * FROM people WHERE phone = NULL;
rules.right: SELECT * FROM people WHERE phone IS NULL;
rules.tip: = NULL is never true. IS NULL is the way.

sample.code: SELECT name FROM people WHERE phone = NULL;
sample.setup: CREATE TABLE people (name TEXT, phone TEXT); INSERT INTO people VALUES ('Asha', '98'), ('Ravi', NULL);

rules.title: WHERE can't filter on a total
rules.say: “WHERE works on COUNT and SUM too.”
rules.truth: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped. To filter on a group's total, use HAVING after GROUP BY.
rules.wrong: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM people WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY city;
rules.right: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM people GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
rules.tip: Rows: WHERE. Groups: HAVING.

sample.code: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM people WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY city;
sample.setup: CREATE TABLE people (name TEXT, city TEXT); INSERT INTO people VALUES ('a','Pune'),('b','Pune'),('c','Goa');

rules.title: Text values need quotes
rules.say: “WHERE city = Pune works without quotes.”
rules.truth: Without quotes, SQL thinks Pune is a column name. Put text in single quotes: 'Pune'.
rules.wrong: SELECT * FROM people WHERE city = Pune;
rules.tip: Words are names; 'words' in quotes are text.

sample.code: SELECT name FROM people WHERE city = Pune;
sample.setup: CREATE TABLE people (name TEXT, city TEXT); INSERT INTO people VALUES ('a','Pune'),('b','Pune'),('c','Goa');
